'''''Stachytarpheta cayennensis''''' is a species of flowering plant in the [[Verbenaceae|verbena family]] known by many [[English language]] common names, including '''blue snakeweed''', '''Cayenne snakeweed''', '''dark-blue snakeweed''', '''bluetop''', '''nettle-leaf porterweed''', '''rattail''', '''rough-leaf false vervain''',<ref name=grin>{{GRIN | access-date = 21 January 2018}}</ref> '''blue rat's tail''', '''Brazilian tea''', '''Cayenne vervain''', '''false verbena''', '''joee''', '''nettleleaf velvetberry''',<ref name=pier>[http://www.hear.org/pier/species/stachytarpheta_cayennensis.htm ''Stachytarpheta cayennensis''.] US Forest Service. Pacific Island Ecosystems at Risk (PIER).</ref> and '''Cayenne porterweed'''.<ref name=nrcs>[ftp://ftp-fc.sc.egov.usda.gov/HI/pub/technotes/Range_&_Pasture/RP_TechNote_3/1_TechNote3_FactSheet-01_Stachytarpheta_cayennensis.pdf Joee (''Stachytarpheta cayennensis'').]{{dead link|date=May 2025|bot=medic}}{{cbignore|bot=medic}} Invasive Species Fact Sheet, Pacific Islands Area. USDA NRCS. 2011.</ref> Names in other languages include '''''honagasō''''' ([[Japanese language|Japanese]]), '''''gervão-urticante''''' ([[Brazilian Portuguese]]),<ref name=grin/> '''''piche de gato''''', '''''rabo de zorro''''' ([[Spanish language|Spanish]]), '''''herbe à chenille''''', '''''herbe bleue''''', '''''queue de rat''''' ([[french language|French]]), '''''ōi''''' or '''''ōwī''''' ([[Hawaiian language|Hawaiian]]), '''''sakura''''' or '''''ouchung''''' ([[Chuukese language|Chuukese]]),<ref name=pier/> and '''''tiāki''''' ([[Māori language|Māori]]).<ref name=pier/> It is native to the Americas, from [[Mexico]] south through Central and South America to [[Argentina]], as well as many islands of the [[Caribbean]]. It is known in many other parts of the world as an [[introduced species]], including regions in Africa, [[India]], [[Indonesia]], [[Australia]], [[Florida]] in the United States, and many [[Pacific Islands]]. Its distribution is now considered [[pantropical]]. In many places, such as [[New Caledonia]],<ref>{{Cite book|url=http://horizon.documentation.ird.fr/exl-doc/pleins_textes/divers12-08/010052239.pdf|title=Les espèces exotiques envahissantes de Nouvelle-Calédonie|last=Hequet|first=Vanessa|year=2009|pages=17, 46|language=fr}}</ref> it has become an [[invasive species]].<ref name=pier/>
[[File:Stachytarpheta cayennensis 6.jpg|thumb|White flowered form]]
This plant is a perennial herb or [[shrub]] growing up to 2<ref name=pier/> or 2.5<ref name=fz>Fernandes, R. [http://apps.kew.org/efloras/namedetail.do?flora=fz&taxon=11532&nameid=29324 ''Stachytarpheta cayennensis''.] ''Flora Zambesiaca'' volume 8, part 7. 2005. Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew.</ref> meters tall. It has an upright, branching stem, sometimes with a woody base. The leaves are oppositely arranged. The blades are up to 8 to 10  centimeters long, oval in shape with sharply toothed edges, and rough-textured or wrinkly on the upper surfaces. The [[inflorescence]] is a very narrow spike up to 40<ref name=pier/> to 45<ref name=fz/> centimeters long covered in pointed [[bract]]s. Occasional flower corollas bloom from between the bracts. The flowers are deep purple-blue to lavender with pale centers,<ref name=pier/> and white-flowered plants are known.<ref name=fz/><ref name=hyde>Hyde, M. A., et al. (2013). [http://www.zimbabweflora.co.zw/speciesdata/species.php?species_id=148800 Species information: ''Stachytarpheta cayennensis''.] Flora of Zimbabwe.</ref> The flowers last a single day before wilting.<ref name=brown>Brown, S. H. and K. Cooprider. [http://lee.ifas.ufl.edu/Hort/GardenPubsAZ/Blue_porterweed.pdf ''Stachytarpheta jamaicensis''.] Lee County. University of Florida, IFAS Extension.</ref> The plant was named for [[Cayenne]], the capital of [[French Guiana]].<ref name=hyde/>

In some places this plant is simply naturalized. It may be a casual weed, a "garden thug", a crop pest, or an invasive species with effects on the local ecosystem.<ref name=gcw>[http://www.hear.org/gcw/species/stachytarpheta_cayennensis/ ''Stachytarpheta cayennensis''.] Global Compendium of Weeds. Hawaiian Ecosystems at Risk (HEAR). 2007.</ref> It is well-adapted to disturbed, cultivated, and wasted land. It grows in pastures, on cropland, and on roadsides. In [[grazing|grazed]] fields it propagates rapidly because livestock find it distasteful, avoid it, and selectively graze out the other vegetation. In rainy areas it can form thick beds, but it easily persists in dry areas.<ref name=pier/>

In Florida, this ''Stachytarpheta'' is often confused with a closely related native species, ''[[Stachytarpheta jamaicensis|S. jamaicensis]]''. It has appealing flower displays that attract [[butterfly|butterflies]]; in its native range it was observed to attract 98 different species.<ref name=fon>Fonseca, N. G., et al. (2006). [http://www.scielo.br/scielo.php?script=sci_arttext&pid=S0085-56262006000300010 Lepidópteros visitantes florais de ''Stachytarpheta cayennensis'' (Rich.) Vahl (Verbenaceae) em remanescente de Mata Atlântica, Minas Gerais, Brasil.] ''Revista Brasileira de Entomologia'' 50(3) 399-405.</ref> It is mistakenly sold as the native [[ornamental plant|ornamental]], planted, and allowed to take hold. It then has the potential to become a [[noxious weed]]. [[Hybrid (biology)|Hybrids]] of the two species also occur when it is introduced.<ref name=brown/><ref name=caip>[http://plants.ifas.ufl.edu/node/438 ''Stachytarpheta urticifolia'' (syn. ''S. cayennensis'').] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150518014105/http://plants.ifas.ufl.edu/node/438 |date=2015-05-18 }} Center for Aquatic and Invasive Plants. University of Florida, IFAS.</ref> Intentional plantings for ornamental purposes are a common way that this plant spreads. It is also introduced when the seed is transported in garden waste, rainwater, [[fodder]], and contaminated seed shipments, and on vehicles.<ref name=pier/>

Methods of control include keeping the plants cut down or pulling them up, taking care to remove the large roots. [[Herbicide]]s such as [[glyphosate]] are used.<ref name=pier/>

This plant has some uses in [[traditional medicine]]. Several Latin American peoples recognize extracts of the plant as a treatment to ease the symptoms of [[malaria]]. The boiled juice or a tea made from the leaves or the whole plant is taken to relieve [[fever]] and other symptoms. It is also used for [[dysentery]], [[pain]], and [[liver]] disorders.<ref name=froe>Froelich, S., et al. (2008). [http://www.scielo.br/scielo.php?pid=S0102-695X2008000400003&script=sci_arttext Phenylethanoid glycosides from ''Stachytarpheta cayennensis'' (Rich.) Vahl, Verbenaceae, a traditional antimalarial medicinal plant.] ''Revista Brasileira de Farmacognosia'' 18(4) 517-20.</ref> A tea of the leaves is taken to help control [[diabetes mellitus|diabetes]] in [[Peru]] and other areas.<ref name=ade>Adebajo, A. C., et al. (2007). [https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17318784 Hypoglycaemic constituents of ''Stachytarpheta cayennensis'' leaf.] ''Planta Med'' 73(3) 241-50.</ref> Laboratory tests indicate that the plant has [[anti-inflammatory]] properties.<ref name=sch>Schapoval, E. E., et al. (1998). [https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9533432 Antiinflammatory and antinociceptive activities of extracts and isolated compounds from ''Stachytarpheta cayennensis''.] ''J Ethnopharmacol.'' 60(1) 53-9.</ref>
